tier_reason: First-party README numbers against nfroidure ttf2woff2 v8.0.0 on an Apple M1 Max, with the harness public in bench/benchmark.cjs (10 timed calls after 3 warmups). rustc, wasm-bindgen, Node versions and the baseline's build are not stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: WarpnineSans-Regular.ttf (269.1 KB): native avg 1331 ms vs wasm avg 500 ms (2.7x faster); NotoSansJP-Medium.ttf (5.5 MB): 19039 ms vs 9756 ms (2.0x faster). The README's '2.2x / 2.6x less memory' figures are JS heap deltas (44.8 KB vs 20.6 KB, 30.0 KB vs 11.4 KB) and do not measure conversion memory. Installed size 968 KB vs 11 MB.
corrections.baseline: ttf2woff2 v8.0.0 (nfroidure/ttf2woff2 npm package, a Node wrapper of Google's woff2 C++ built with node-gyp at install, falling back to an Emscripten build if compilation fails; labelled 'native' in the benchmark output)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: wasm side: Cargo release profile opt-level="s", lto=true (Cargo.toml), built via cargo xtask; rustc, wasm-bindgen and Node versions not stated; baseline built by node-gyp defaults
corrections.workload: TTF to WOFF2 conversion at Brotli quality 11 on both sides of two fonts (269.1 KB WarpnineSans-Regular and 5.5 MB NotoSansJP-Medium), average of 10 timed calls after 3 warmups per implementation (bench/benchmark.cjs).
corrections.caveats: First-party, 1-star wrapper; the conversion core is the author's pure-Rust crate 0x6b/ttf2woff2 (Rust brotli crate v9), exposed through wasm-bindgen. Both sides compress at Brotli quality 11 (the wasm wrapper defaults to 11), but the benchmark neither compares output sizes nor validates the output, and the README warns the output differs in size from nfroidure/ttf2woff2. The 'native' label is unverified: ttf2woff2's npm install script runs node-gyp and silently falls back to an Emscripten build on failure, and the script does not report which path loaded. The 'less memory' figures are process.memoryUsage().heapUsed deltas, which exclude native-addon malloc and wasm linear memory, so they say nothing about real memory use. The speedup comes mostly from the Rust Brotli encoder, not from wasm: the core crate's README shows Rust q11 at 3.25 s versus fonttools (C brotli) at 9.86 s on the same NotoSansJP font with near-identical output size (Apple M4 Pro). Single machine, Node version not stated.

notes: The README numbers match the bench/benchmark.cjs output format exactly, and the baseline is the named incumbent npm package. Shortcomings: memory claim invalid (JS heap delta only), 'native' baseline path unverified (node-gyp with silent Emscripten fallback), no output-size or correctness check, and the win comes from the Rust Brotli encoder rather than wasm. The core crate 0x6b/ttf2woff2 (11 stars) may be the better catalog target for native use.

tier_reason: First-party README highlights against math.js on a Mac mini M1; the harness is public (scripts/benchmark.ts, run by deno task benchmark) but the math.js version is unpinned and rustc/Deno versions are not stated, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile opt-level="z", lto=true, codegen-units=1 (Cargo.toml), built with deno wasmbuild (jsr:@deno/wasmbuild); rustc, Deno and math.js versions not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers; GitHub lists the repo as a fork of maxto/ubique, and v1.0 is a full rewrite on nalgebra compiled to wasm. The harness is scripts/benchmark.ts: it imports npm:mathjs unversioned, times one loop per test (5 iterations for the 500x500 multiply, 50-200 elsewhere) on fresh random inputs with no warmup, and always times Ubique first. It checks results against math.js to 6 decimals. The README shows 6 highlight rows out of the suite's 17 (statistics rows and the 10x10/50x50/100x100 multiply and 10x10 inverse rows are not reported), so selective reporting is possible. The wasm is built for size (opt-level z) without SIMD flags. math.js is a generic pure-JS library, not a tuned JS linear-algebra baseline. The github.io interactive benchmark page could not be opened here.

notes: The README numbers (13.05x, 6.61x, 4.63x, 26.04x, 7.53x, 12.27x on a Mac mini M1) match the record; the benchmark source exists at scripts/benchmark.ts, which the search agent missed. Shortcomings: unpinned math.js version, no warmup, single timed loop, only 6 of 17 suite rows reported, weak generic JS baseline, 5 stars. GitHub shows 'forked from maxto/ubique' (now a rewrite).

tier_reason: First-party README table against the ulid npm package on an Apple M2 Pro, with the Benchmark.js harness public in benchmark.js; rustc version and run conditions are not stated (Node 20.12.2 is only pinned in .node-version), so not A.

corrections.baseline: ulid 2.x (ulid/javascript, the reference pure-JavaScript ULID generator; devDependency ^2.3.0)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack build --target web --release with Cargo release lto=true; .node-version pins Node 20.12.2; rustc version not stated
corrections.workload: ULID generation (ulid(), monotonicFactory()) and time encode/decode, ops/sec measured with Benchmark.js in Node (benchmark.js, pnpm benchmark).
corrections.caveats: First-party, 4 commits, untouched since May 2024. The 43x ulid() row measures random-number batching, not wasm codegen: ulid 2.3.0 calls Node crypto.randomBytes(1) once per character (16 calls and Buffer allocations per ULID), while wa-ulid fills the 16 characters from rand::thread_rng (a userspace ChaCha12 CSPRNG seeded once through getrandom's js feature). Both are cryptographically secure, so the row is a real API-level win, but a JS implementation that batches getRandomValues would close most of the gap (not measured). The README's statement that randomness does not use browser or Node crypto APIs is only true per call; the seed comes from them through getrandom. The other rows are 1.27x-2.73x. A user-supplied PRNG path calls back into JS once per character and was not benchmarked. Single machine; numbers not reproduced independently.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (44,758 vs 1,933,859 ops/s = 43.20x; 2.73x, 1.47x, 1.27x). Shortcomings: the headline 43x comes from the baseline's per-character crypto.randomBytes(1) calls versus a buffered in-wasm ChaCha12 RNG, first-party only, stale (last commit 2024-05-11), 21 stars.
